332.text: Unlike its more common literal sense of persons being 'idle/lazy' (e.g. idle in the marketplace, Mt 20:3,6), here the adjective is applied metaphorically to faith itself as an abstraction, describing its ineffectiveness rather than a person's laziness.

337.text: Idleness (G0692) directly predicates faith (M13) as inoperative apart from works; it relates to the wanting/knowing verbs (G2309, G1097) only as the content to be recognized, not as a party-sharing characteristic itself -- its core tight relation remains with M13, same party (the professed believer).

338.text: No operation/role-T3 word is present in Jas 2:20 alongside a party tag in direct relation to G0692; the verb 'is' (copula) carries no operational force.

586.text: G0692 functions as the negative pole of the M67 cluster, spanning literal unemployment (Matt 20:3,6), habitual moral laziness (1 Tim 5:13; Titus 1:12), and metaphorical spiritual unfruitfulness (2 Pet 1:8; Jas 2:20) -- the broadest and most semantically flexible term in the cluster.

594.text: Within its own 8 occurrences, G0692 shows the same negative-pole 'not-working' core as G0691 and H8220, but uniquely spans the full range from wholly literal/circumstantial idleness (Matt.20.3,6 -- unemployed day-laborers awaiting hire, a neutral economic state) to morally-loaded habitual laziness (1Tim.5.13; Titus.1.12) to fully metaphorical spiritual unfruitfulness (2Pet.1.8; Jas.2.20) to careless/culpable speech (Matt.12.36) -- making it the semantic bridge connecting the concrete physical sense shared with H8220 and the abstract personification sense shared with G0691.

667.text: The evidence does not establish a consistent precede/follow pattern relative to judgement or belief. In Matt.20.6 idleness precedes a challenge/question (which functions as address, not judgement per se); in Jas.2.20 'useless' functions as a conclusion about faith reached through argument (following an implied judgement); in 2Pet.2.3 'not idle' asserts the ongoing operation of a prior judgement (condemnation) rather than preceding or following a discrete belief-act. Signal: this may resolve further with adjacent-verse context on the argument structures in James and 2 Peter.

672.text: Yes, the mechanism differs sharply by context: in Eccl.10.18 idleness operates through bodily/instrumental neglect (slack hands failing to maintain a structure, producing physical decay); in Matt.20.3,6 it operates as an economic/circumstantial state (lack of an employer/opportunity) reversed by verbal address and assignment; in 1Tim.5.13/Titus.1.12 it operates as a habitual moral-social vice generating further vices (gossip, meddling); in 2Pet.1.8/Jas.2.20 it operates metaphorically as spiritual unfruitfulness/uselessness of qualities or faith; in 2Pet.2.3 it operates as personified negation describing the unceasing operation of divine judgement.

675.text: Yes -- mode varies: literal/physical (Matt.20.3,6 -- standing unemployed; Eccl.10.18 -- slack hands causing structural decay), social-habitual (1Tim.5.13; Titus.1.12 -- persons characterized as idlers/gluttons), verbal-moral (Matt.12.36 -- careless words), spiritual-metaphorical (2Pet.1.8 -- ineffective in knowledge; Jas.2.20 -- useless faith), and abstract-personified (2Pet.2.3 -- condemnation not idle). Constitutional level ranges from bodily/hand-instrumental (H8220) to purely predicated-abstract (G0691).

677.text: Idleness/uselessness takes hold rightly (i.e. is rightly named/exposed) under conditions of neglect: slack hands (Eccl.10.18), lack of assigned work/opportunity (Matt.20.3,6), habitual house-to-house wandering without occupation (1Tim.5.13), and absence of works accompanying professed faith (Jas.2.20). Inwardly, its 'proper' operation (as a negative diagnostic) requires an underlying absence of diligence, zeal, or productive engagement.

682.text: The relational scope is universal in principle -- idleness/uselessness is applied to Jewish day-laborers, Gentile Cretans, Christian widows, and abstract qualities (faith, condemnation) alike, with no ethnic, gender, or covenantal exclusion visible in the evidence; the only consistent exclusion is from those actively engaged in productive labor, virtue, or works.

684.text: None -- the subgroup's evidence does not depict a human-to-God movement associated with idleness/indolence; the characteristic is descriptive of human or abstract states, not itself a movement toward God.

688.text: Where idleness is present in a person (1Tim.5.13; Titus.1.12) or where useless faith lacks works (Jas.2.20), it indicates diminished or unrealized expression of the divine image's active/relational capacities; where it is absent and replaced by increasing virtue (2Pet.1.8), the image's fruitful function is evidenced as intact and growing.

699.text: The origin is multiple and context-dependent: circumstantial/economic (lack of a hiring employer, Matt.20.3,6), habitual/social (learned through idle house-to-house wandering, 1Tim.5.13), cultural-ethnic stereotype (Titus.1.12), spiritual deficiency (absence of increasing virtue, 2Pet.1.8), evidential absence of works (Jas.2.20), physical neglect (slack hands, Eccl.10.18), and rhetorical personification (2Pet.2.3). No single origin is uniform.

700.text: The faculties most engaged are the will/behavior (standing idle, going about, engaging or not in work) and speech (careless words, Matt.12.36; direct address, Matt.20.6), with the intellect/faith-conviction faculty engaged metaphorically in Jas.2.20 (faith without works). The affections/emotions are never engaged -- no occurrence attaches feeling-language to idleness, indicating the characteristic's nature is behavioral/volitional and evidentiary (visible in outward act or its absence) rather than affective.

704.text: At its edge, the characteristic excludes/resists productive labor, fruitful spiritual growth, and useful/effective works -- it is defined precisely by the negation and absence of these things (2Pet.1.8's 'ineffective or unfruitful'; Jas.2.20's 'useless...apart from works').

706.text: Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside idleness: sloth/H6103 (Eccl.10.18, synonymous parallelism); hand/body-instrument language (H3027-related, Eccl.10.18); gossip and busybodiness (1Tim.5.13); lying and evil-beast character (Titus.1.12, tricolon of vices); knowledge/virtue-list qualities (2Pet.1.8); faith and works (Jas.2.20); condemnation and destruction/'not asleep' (2Pet.2.3, synonymous parallel negation). These co-occurrences are frequent and consistently pair idleness with either vice-clusters or growth/virtue-clusters as its counterpoint.

708.text: Yes -- idleness precedes and generates further vice in 1Tim.5.13 (idleness -> gossip/busybodiness) and in Eccl.10.18 (indolent hands -> house decay); it is diagnostically dependent on/follows the absence of works in Jas.2.20 (faith without works -> shown to be useless). In Matt.20.3,6 idleness precedes and is resolved by being hired into work.

709.text: The sequence is causal in Eccl.10.18 and 1Tim.5.13 (idleness mechanically/socially produces decay or further vice) and diagnostic/correlational in Jas.2.20 (absence of works correlates with and evidences dead faith, rather than causing it). In Matt.20.3-6 the sequence is developmental -- idleness resolved into productive engagement through the householder's initiative.

10009.text: Located at the level of the mind/understanding of the addressed person.

10010.text: Originates from another person (James) demonstrating/teaching the truth to the addressee.

10011.text: Faith here is stated as the very thing that must be joined to works or else it is rendered useless -- its purpose/effect is what is under scrutiny.

10012.text: Faith engages volition and moral evaluation -- it is presented as a professed conviction that must be paired with active moral response (works).

10013.text: Faith is the person's professed trust/belief oriented toward God, but the verse shows it as inert apart from works -- a deficient form of that movement.

10014.text: The verse does not depict faith here as an operation from God toward the person, but as the person's own held/professed state being evaluated.

10015.text: Faith is not depicted as extended from one person to another in this verse.

10016.text: Faith is not shown here as taken up from another person; it is the addressee's own possessed (but inert) faith.

10017.text: No relation to angelic or adversarial spiritual beings is shown for faith in this verse.

10018.text: Faith is related to God as its proper object/orientation, though the verse's focus is that such faith, apart from works, fails to be operative.

10019.text: No immediate inner response following from faith is described here; the verse instead states a negative condition (uselessness) about faith itself.

10020.text: No positive inner-being production is shown; the verse instead flags this faith's failure to be effective without accompanying works.

10021.text: The verse implies faith's condition (whether it is living/effective or dead/useless) depends on the presence of works, but does not itself narrate a change occurring -- it states a diagnostic condition.

10022.text: No sequence of inner states through faith is depicted here.

10023.text: No mechanism of change in the person is shown; the verse states a condition about faith's uselessness rather than a formation process.

10024.text: Faith operates here as a professed conviction/disposition mode, evaluated for whether it issues in action.

10025.text: Located at the level of heart/mind conviction -- the professed inner trust that this verse tests against outward works.

10026.text: The verse does not state faith's origin here; it is simply presupposed as possessed by the addressee.

10027.text: The interjection "you" (O, vocative particle) is purely a supporting exclamatory marker addressing the foolish person, not a candidate for its own inner-being characteristic.

10028.text: "Foolish" functions here as a vocative qualifier describing the addressee's lack of understanding, a supporting descriptor for the rhetorical rebuke rather than its own distinct characteristic.

10029.text: "Apart from" is a prepositional qualifier specifying the separation of faith from works, not itself a characteristic.

10030.text: "Works" here functions as the counterpart term faith is measured against; it names a concrete category of deeds, a supporting term rather than an inner-being characteristic in its own right in this verse's usage.

10031.text: The copula "is" is a linking verb joining faith and useless; purely grammatical, not a candidate characteristic.

11610.text: Surface 'want' (V-PAI-2S, present active) shows James addressing the reader directly, naming a present act of will/desire to be shown proof, not a settled disposition.

11611.text: Here it means to be willing/wish, introducing a rhetorical demand: the reader is asked whether he wishes to have it demonstrated that faith without works is useless.

11612.text: The willing here is directional: it points the addressee toward receiving proof/demonstration, setting up the argument that follows rather than expressing an independent desire of its own content.

11613.text: Root sense 'to exercise the will, be willing' operates here as the trigger verb introducing the rhetorical question that drives the passage's argument.

11614.text: The sense matches the term's usual 'wish/be willing' use with a following infinitive-type construction; no divergence from ordinary usage here.

11615.text: Present active indicative 2nd singular shows an ongoing, direct address to 'you' the foolish person, framing this as a live rhetorical challenge in the moment of speaking.

11616.text: Within its range (wish, be inclined, intend, choose), this occurrence sits at the basic 'wish/desire' sense governing a following demonstration, a common rhetorical usage.

11617.text: This occurrence expresses an act (a present wish/desire being voiced), not a fixed disposition or condition.

11618.text: No structural opposite among G2309's related terms is relevant to this occurrence's plain rhetorical use of 'want to be shown'.

11619.text: No person-type term (one who habitually wills/desires) is relevant to this occurrence, which is a simple verb of address, not a naming of character trait.

11620.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the verb simply expresses the addressee's own wish, not a request directed at another.

11621.text: As an NT Greek occurrence in a direct rhetorical address, Testament context (NT vs OT) makes no interpretive difference to this common volitional verb here.

11622.text: Thelo/ethelo is attested well before the NT period (Homer onward per LSJ); this occurrence is an ordinary classical-continuous use, not a NT coinage.

11623.text: Surface 'shown' (V-2AAN, aorist passive-form infinitive of ginosko) names the essential act of being made to know/perceive -- the reader is to be given knowledge, not simply told.

11624.text: Here it means to come to know/perceive by demonstration -- James wants the fool to be brought to a realized understanding that faith apart from works is useless.

11625.text: The term carries a directional force here: knowledge is to be brought TO the addressee via demonstration, moving him from ignorance to recognized understanding of the claim about faith and works.

11626.text: Root sense 'to know/come to know, perceive' operates here as the goal-verb of the rhetorical question -- the addressee is to be brought to perceive a truth by demonstration.

11627.text: This use matches the term's usual 'come to know/perceive' sense via demonstration; no divergence from its ordinary NT usage here.

11628.text: Aorist active infinitive form shows a single, completed act of coming-to-know being sought for the addressee, dependent on the governing verb 'want'.

11629.text: Within its range (perceive, ascertain, understand, acknowledge), this occurrence sits at 'to be shown/made to understand by demonstration,' a common evidential use.

11630.text: This occurrence expresses an act -- the act of coming to know/being shown -- rather than a fixed disposition or condition.

11631.text: No structural opposite among G1097's related terms is relevant to this occurrence's use as the verb of demonstrative knowing.

11632.text: No person-type term is relevant here; the verb names an act of being brought to knowledge, not a habitual character trait.

11633.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant; the verb expresses coming-to-know, not petitioning another for it.

11634.text: As an NT Greek occurrence in ordinary demonstrative usage, Testament context makes no interpretive difference to this occurrence's plain sense.

11635.text: Ginosko/gignosko is attested from Homer onward per LSJ; this occurrence is an ordinary continuation of classical usage, not a NT coinage.

11636.text: Surface 'faith' (N-NSF, nominative singular feminine) names the subject of the clause -- faith itself is being characterized (as useless when apart from works), showing its essential nature as a state that must be paired with action to have effect.

11637.text: Here it means firm persuasion/belief -- specifically the professed trust in God that James contrasts with accompanying deeds; without works, this belief is declared useless.

11638.text: The term's relational implication here is that faith is constitutionally meant to be joined with works; named 'apart from works' it is shown as incomplete/inert on its own.

11639.text: Root sense 'trust, persuasion' (from peithomai) operates here as a disposition of the person which, when isolated from works, is declared ineffective/useless.

11640.text: This occurrence matches the term's usual NT theological sense (belief/trust in God), presented in its ordinary abstract-noun form; no divergence from that sense here.

11641.text: Nominative singular feminine noun form shows faith functioning as the grammatical subject being evaluated/qualified by the predicate 'useless apart from works'.

11642.text: Within its range (trust, faithfulness, ground of belief), this occurrence sits at the theological sense of professed belief/trust in God, evaluated for whether it produces action.

11643.text: This occurrence expresses a disposition/condition (a state of belief held) rather than an act, being evaluated for its lack of accompanying action.

11644.text: Works (ergon, T2 term 'works' in this verse) functions as the structural counterpart/opposite pole here -- faith is declared useless precisely 'apart from' works.

11645.text: No person-type term (one who habitually has faith) is directly relevant to this occurrence, which evaluates faith itself in the abstract, not a person's character.

11646.text: No supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the verse evaluates faith's effect rather than the act of seeking faith from another.

11647.text: The NT theological sense of pistis (belief/trust in God/Christ) governs this occurrence, distinct from the term's more general classical Greek senses of pledge or credit; that NT-specific sense is what is being tested against works here.

11648.text: Pistis is attested from Hesiod onward per LSJ, with classical senses of trust/pledge/proof predating the NT; this occurrence continues and narrows that established word to its NT theological use.

11649.text: Surface 'useless' (A-NSF, nominative singular feminine adjective) predicates faith itself, showing this occurrence's essential nature as marking faith-without-works as inert/unproductive -- the negative pole of the idle-vs-active cluster.

11650.text: Here it means unprofitable/ineffective -- faith apart from works produces nothing, per the lexicon's 'unprofitable, hollow, ineffective' sense applied specifically to this verse.

11651.text: The term's implication here is constitutional: faith without works fails to constitute genuine, functioning faith -- it lacks the productive outworking that would make it real/effective.

11652.text: Root sense 'not working, idle' (a-ergos, 'without work') operates literally here: faith lacking works is 'not-working,' unproductive faith.

11653.text: Nominative singular feminine adjective agrees with and predicates 'faith,' grammatically marking faith itself as the thing characterized as useless/inert.

11654.text: Within its range (inactive, idle, unprofitable, careless), this occurrence sits at the metaphorical 'unprofitable/ineffective' end, applied to faith rather than to a person's labor.

11655.text: This occurrence expresses a quality/condition attributed to faith (its uselessness) rather than an act.

11656.text: Works (ergon) is the structural opposite here -- 'useless' names exactly the state faith falls into when works are absent, making ergon its direct counterpart term.

11657.text: No person-type term (a habitually idle person) is relevant here since the adjective modifies faith, an abstraction, not a person's character.

11658.text: No supplication/seeking term applies; this occurrence describes a state of ineffectiveness, not an act of seeking something from another.

11659.text: As an NT Greek occurrence used in ordinary metaphorical extension of a classical adjective, Testament context makes no additional interpretive difference here beyond the metaphorical application itself.

11660.text: Argos is attested from at least the 5th century BC (Herodotus, Sophocles, etc. per LSJ) with established senses of idle/lazy/unproductive; this verse's metaphorical use of that established term is not a NT coinage.

19061.text: The verses: *"our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you"* (10:8). *"I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters"* (10:9).; *"that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down"* (13:10). The verses before: *"we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for"* (13:9).

19146.text: Luk 10:19–20. *"Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven."*

19641.text: Jeremiah 33:24: "'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people": *"Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (v24).; Others look at the state of the chosen and draw a conclusion about God: he has rejected them. Their contempt rests on that conclusion. "Despised" is *nāʾaṣ* (*to spurn*; H5006). The measure is their own: *"in their sight"*. "Rejected" is *māʾas* (H3988A), the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15 (§2a).; God answers with the fixed order of creation: *"If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule"* (v25–26). It ends: *"For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them"* (v26).

19654.text: Isaiah 1:29 — "the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen": The oracle also holds out the other side to those who turn: *"Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness"* (v27). The Lord will *"smelt away your dross"* and *"restore"* (v25–26). The choice is not closed off at the first wrong choosing. The offer of v18 stands in the middle of the charge.; Elsewhere in Isaiah, gardens are places of the worship the Lord rejects: *"sacrificing in gardens"* (65:3), *"those who … go into the gardens … eating pig’s flesh"* (66:17). It is the same word (H1593). That fills in what the figure draws on; the figure in 1:29 does not need it to be understood.

20128.text: The epistle openings and requests (*"I want you to know"*, Phi 1:12; Tit 3:8; Jude 5; 1Ti 2:8; 5:14; 2Jo 12; Phm 13; 3Jo 10) mostly use the word as a stated wish in teaching. Their bearing on setting direction is slight, but each still needs to be read.

20138.text: The willing heart (*nāḏîḇ*, H5081G, 5 verses) is the will freely given: *"Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the Lord's contribution"* (Exo 35:5); *"All who were of a willing heart brought"* (Exo 35:22; also 2Ch 29:31; 1Ch 28:21); It is asked of God: *"uphold me with a willing spirit"* (Psa 51:12).; 10.7 *Setting the heart* already cites Exo 35:21, *"everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"*, the verse just before 35:22.

20167.text: Moved from inside: *"they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exo 35:21), then *"All who were of a willing heart brought"* (35:22). Moses had said *"Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring"* (35:5).

20186.text: Paul's wishes for the churches are mostly stated wishes in teaching. Their passages give each one a reason: *"I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling"* (1Ti 2:8); *"I would have younger widows marry … for some have already strayed after Satan"* (1Ti 5:14–15); *"I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works"* (Tit 3:8); *"I want you to know … what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel"* (Phi 1:12); *"I would rather not use paper and ink … talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete"* (2Jo 12); *"I want to remind you"* (Jude 5)

20211.text: The heart and spirit named with the act.; Planning: *"The heart of man plans his way"* (Pro 16:9); *"plan evil things in their heart"* (Psa 140:2).; Willing: the heart or spirit hardened, stubborn or lifted up (Exo 10:27; Deu 2:30; Eze 3:7; Psa 81:12; Deu 29:19; Dan 5:20); the willing heart and spirit (Exo 35:21–22; 2Ch 29:31; Psa 51:12).; So the will verses name the state of the heart and spirit more often than the plan verses do. Chapters 4 (the heart) and 6 (the spirit) should take this.

20282.text: John 15:19: "but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you": Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his death. The passage begins with love among the chosen: *"This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you"* (v12). The choosing is said twice: *"You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit"* (v16); *"If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (v19); The world's two inner acts are set side by side. "Love" is *phileō* (G5368): the world loves *"its own"*. "Hates" is *miseō* (G3404). The verse says the hatred is *because* of the choosing: *"I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"*.; The passage says the hatred was first aimed at Jesus: *"If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you"* (v18). It gives a reason in the haters: *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (v21). It says they have *"seen and hated both me and my Father"* (v24), and *"They hated me without a cause"* (v25).; Beside the world's hatred stands the command given twice to the chosen: *"love one another"* (v12, v17).

20283.text: Acts 15:7: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe": The chapter is the dispute over circumcision: *"no small dissension and debate"* (v2), then *"much debate"* among the apostles and elders (v7). Peter stands up and appeals to what they already know: *"Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (v7).; "Know" is *epistamai* (G1987). Their knowing of a past choice by God is the ground Peter argues from. The purpose of that choice lies in others: *"that … the Gentiles should hear … and believe"* (*pisteuō*, G4100).; Peter goes on to the Gentiles' hearts: *"God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us"* (v8); *"he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith"* (v9); *"why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?"* (v10); The debate ends: *"And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened"* (v12). The assembly's own choosing follows later in the chapter: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men"* (v25). That was read for §2a.

20284.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: God's choosing of one man has its purpose in others: that the Gentiles hear and believe.; Knowing that God has chosen is the ground on which a dispute is settled.; The Gentiles' hearts are known by God and cleansed by faith (v8–9). God's knowing is rule 72, A. The cleansing of their hearts is in the human inner being.; The debate gives way to silence and listening (v12).

20285.text: Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened": Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers: *"By no means!"* (v1). *"God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew"* (v2). He gives Elijah, who thought he was alone, and God's reply: *"I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal"* (v4). *"So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"* (v5–6).; Then v7: *"What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"*.; The others are *"the rest"*. Two things are said of them: They were seeking (*epizēteō*, G1934) and did not obtain.; They were hardened (*pōroō*, G4456).; The hardening is described from Scripture: *"God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day"* (v8). The giving is God's act (rule 72, A). The eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear are in the human inner being.; Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

20290.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: A person endures suffering for the sake of the chosen.; The aim is their salvation: *"that they also may obtain"*.; The same endurance is promised its outcome: *"if we endure, we will also reign with him"* (v12).

20291.text: 1 Peter 2:4: "a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious": The chapter opens with what the readers are to put away and to long for: *"So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk"* (v1–2).; Then: *"As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (v4).; Two measures stand in one verse: *"rejected by men"* and *"in the sight of God chosen"*. "Rejected" is *apodokimazō* (G0593), to reject after testing. The quotation in v7 uses the same word: *"The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone"*.; The readers share the same name: *"you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation"* (v9). They will be spoken against in turn: *"when they speak against you as evildoers"* (v12).
